Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: The assault happened on a Tuesday in late October, right at 4:30 p.m., while Sione was tightening the busbars on a new service panel in the back of a downtown community center. He remembered the moment not as a flowing sequence but as a series of sharp photographs: the heavy steel door slamming shut behind him, the blur of two men stepping into the work light, and the sudden grip on his shoulders. When his partner later asked how it had unfolded, Sione found he could only point to those frozen frames. He felt certain that large gaps remained in his account, as though the missing film had been cut from the reel entirely. The sudden pressure of their hands had left him braced against touch, and any unexpected movement nearby still drew a quick, defensive reaction from him. He held the event against his own character, certain it happened to him simply because of the sort of man he was, and someone with sharper instincts or a heavier build would not have ended up pinned against that panel. Afterward, the late afternoon hour became a threshold. Every day at 4:30, the light in his truck would shift, and a quiet detachment would settle over him, making the steering wheel and dashboard feel distant and unreal. He began steering clear of unfamiliar clinics, warehouses, and even new job sites, unable to trust his ability to read the threat in unfamiliar spaces. At work, the habits compounded. Sione spent long hours scrolling through games and social feeds, letting the screen hum drown out the echo of the slam. He paired the quiet hours with a daily ritual of two beers and a prescribed muscle relaxer, keeping the quiet steady. He avoided television and news segments that lingered on street violence, preferring to keep his attention fixed on familiar routines. The avoidance carved a quiet distance into his relationship with his partner, Maya. When she reached out to adjust his collar or tap his arm, he flinched before he could catch himself, retreating into his phone rather than meeting her eyes. His refusal to take on the site supervisor role felt less like a career pause and more like a narrowing of his world. The guilt arrived with the memories. Whenever the late sun hit the window at 4:30, or a heavy door echoed down the street, Sione would feel a sharp, familiar weight in his chest. He blamed his own character for the event, convinced that his quiet nature had made him an easy target, and that the guilt was his due. Over the months, the hopelessness settled in like a low tide. He watched his days repeat, the future feeling fixed and small, as though the next twenty years would look much like the last few. What kept him moving forward was the quiet accumulation of these moments and the realization that his body was still waiting for a threat that had already passed. At forty-two, with a PCL-5 score that finally pushed him to book an appointment, Sione sat in the waiting room listening to the reception door click open. He was afraid he would spend his life braced for the next grab, but he also hoped, for the first time, that he might be able to step out of the late afternoon shadows and remember the whole picture.
